what: The quality gap in published NHANES research
title: Navigating Variable Name Changes and Analyte Gaps in NHANES
text: NHANES one accessible large-scale epidemiological datasets existence, accessibility generated publication explosion. Suchak et al. (2025) analysed 341 NHANES single-factor analyses published past decade documented sharp acceleration: average four papers per year 2014–2021 190 papers 2024 alone, 92% manuscripts 2021–2024 carrying primary author affiliation China median publishing journal impact factor 3.6. NCHS — agency produces NHANES — responded January 2026 explicit quality framework whose opening statement acknowledges “exponential rise NHANES-based studies raised concerns publication low-quality studies driven freely available data new artificial intelligence tools” (NCHS 2026). methodological failures Suchak et al. documented consistent: analyses restricted narrow date range without justification, failure apply survey weights specify complex survey design variables (PSU strata), single-factor exposure models treat multifactorial outcome one variable explains , correction multiple comparisons. NCHS’s six quality criteria map directly onto failures — correct weight application, incorporation survey design variables, use bridging equations cross-cycle laboratory method changes, justification restricted date range. barrier meeting criteria partly technical: NHANES data distributed hundreds separate SAS transport files inconsistent variable naming across cycles, correctly pooling even handful analytes across full available date range requires resolving dozens file-variable pairs writing single line analysis code. navigation burden makes easier grab single recent cycle convenient variable name assemble full longitudinal record dataset supports. nhanesR designed remove barrier.

what: Two structural barriers to full-cycle, properly-weighted analyses
title: Navigating Variable Name Changes and Analyte Gaps in NHANES
text: NHANES releases data two-year cycles. cycle separate file separate name, variables inside files guaranteed named consistently one cycle next. time, every analyte measured every cycle: added partway survey programme, dropped funding changes, present cycles missing one two reasons always documented. researcher building multi-cycle analytic dataset therefore faces two interleaved problems: Name drift. variable recording given measurement may named differently across cycles — sometimes prefix change (LBXS → LBDS), sometimes case change (MCQ160L → MCQ160l), sometimes completely different name conceptually question. Availability gaps. analyte present seven eight cycles looks like complete data individual cycle requires careful bookkeeping cycles pooled. Assuming analyte present merging SEQN alone silently produce NA missing cycle rather error. Together, problems mean pooling even four eight NHANES cycles multi-analyte analysis requires manually inspecting dozens data dictionaries, tracking file variable lives cycle, writing separate harmonisation code problematic transition. suite eight analytes spanning eight cycles amounts checking reconciling roughly 64 file-variable pairs writing single line analysis code. vignette shows nhanesR addresses problems using realistic example drawn multi-cycle hepatic biomarker mortality analysis.

what: Downloading ALP across all available cycles
title: Navigating Variable Name Changes and Analyte Gaps in NHANES
text: Internally, nhanes_download_analyte() resolves LBXSAPSI / LBDSAPSI prefix ambiguity cycle independently. returned column named ALP (whichever canonical name found first) regardless prefix underlying file uses. researcher never needs know prefix applies cycle.
code: alp_cycles <- c("1999-2000", "2001-2002", "2003-2004",                 "2013-2014", "2015-2016", "2017-2018")  alp_list <- nhanes_download_analyte(   "alkaline phosphatase",   cycles    = alp_cycles,   component = "Laboratory" )  # Each element is a data frame for one cycle lapply(alp_list, head, 3) alp_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(alp_list, function(df) {   # Identify whichever column was returned — LBXSAPSI or LBDSAPSI   v <- intersect(c("LBXSAPSI", "LBDSAPSI"), names(df))   data.frame(     SEQN = as.character(df$SEQN),     ALP  = df[[v[1]]],     stringsAsFactors = FALSE   ) }))  cat("ALP rows:", nrow(alp_df), "  non-NA:", sum(!is.na(alp_df$ALP)), "\n")

code: # Early cycles: uppercase L mcq_early <- nhanes_download_analyte(   "MCQ160L",   cycles    = c("2003-2004", "2005-2006", "2007-2008", "2009-2010"),   component = "Questionnaire" ) df_early <- do.call(rbind, lapply(mcq_early, function(df) {   data.frame(SEQN          = as.character(df$SEQN),              liver_ever    = df$MCQ160L,              liver_current = df$MCQ170L,              stringsAsFactors = FALSE) }))  # Late cycles: lowercase l mcq_late <- nhanes_download_analyte(   "MCQ160l",   cycles    = c("2011-2012", "2013-2014", "2015-2016", "2017-2018"),   component = "Questionnaire" ) df_late <- do.call(rbind, lapply(mcq_late, function(df) {   data.frame(SEQN          = as.character(df$SEQN),              liver_ever    = df$MCQ160l,              liver_current = df$MCQ170l,              stringsAsFactors = FALSE) }))  mcq_df <- rbind(df_early, df_late) cat("Liver disease history rows:", nrow(mcq_df), "\n") cat("Ever reported (code 1):",     sum(mcq_df$liver_ever == 1, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")

what: Example 6: Disambiguation by component — serum versus urine albumin
title: Navigating Variable Name Changes and Analyte Gaps in NHANES
text: subtler naming problem arises generic search term matches variables conceptually different specimen types. Searching “albumin” without specifying component returns results laboratory examination files: results include minimum: measure fundamentally different things. Serum albumin (LBXSAL) reflects hepatic synthetic capacity nutritional status; variable relevant liver function panels MELD-score work. Urinary albumin (URXUMA) reflects glomerular filtration integrity; variable relevant diabetic nephropathy CKD screening. data scientist research assistant unfamiliar clinical laboratory practice may recognise distinct assays distinct specimen types returned generic search term. Specifying component = "Laboratory" narrows results: returns LBXSAL, eliminating urine variable consideration. component argument therefore merely performance optimisation — clinical guard inadvertently merging wrong albumin hepatic renal endpoint analysis.
code: nhanes_search_variables("albumin") nhanes_search_variables("albumin", component = "Laboratory")

title: NHANES Mortality Linkage: A Complete Workflow
text: NHANES (National Health Nutrition Examination Survey) conducted two-year cycles (e.g. 1999–2000, 2001–2002, …, 2017–2018). Within cycle, data organized five components: participant unique identifier, SEQN, links files within cycle. SEQNs reused across cycles, always include "cycle" merge keys pooling multiple cycles.

text: NHANES analytes often stored different variable names different cycles. nhanes_search_variables() searches CDC variable catalog keyword. nhanes_variable_map() returns one-row-per-cycle lookup table showing exact file name variable name use. nhanes_variable_map() output directly informs keep_vars argument used download harmonization .

title: NHANES Mortality Linkage: A Complete Workflow
text: nhanes_harmonize() renames per-cycle variables single common name optionally stacks cycles one data frame. Unit-based harmonization (laboratory data): specify unit name; function finds right column cycle matching label attribute, variable codes needed. prefer_mgdl = TRUE (default) drops mmol/L duplicates automatically. trim = TRUE (default) returns SEQN, cycle, target column — ready merging. Mapping-based harmonization (questionnaire data): use mapping unit match. trim = TRUE default applies.
code: # Total cholesterol — LBXTC throughout, but label_pattern narrows the match # in 1999-2004 when TC and HDL were bundled in the same file TC <- nhanes_harmonize(   tchol_list,   unit          = "mg/dL",   name          = "TC_mgdl",   label_pattern = "total cholesterol" )  # HDL — three different variable names across cycles; unit approach handles all HDL <- nhanes_harmonize(   hdl_list,   unit          = "mg/dL",   name          = "HDL_mgdl",   label_pattern = "HDL" )  str(TC)   # SEQN (chr), cycle (chr), TC_mgdl (num) str(HDL)  # SEQN (chr), cycle (chr), HDL_mgdl (num) MI <- nhanes_harmonize(   mi_list,   mapping = c(MCQ160E = "MI_history", MCQ160e = "MI_history") )  chol_med <- nhanes_harmonize(   chol_med_list,   mapping = c(BPQ090D = "chol_med", BPQ101D = "chol_med") )  # Each result is a trim 3-column data frame ready for merging str(MI)        # SEQN, cycle, MI_history str(chol_med)  # SEQN, cycle, chol_med

text: nhanes_mortality_link() downloads NCHS Public-Use Linked Mortality Files left-joins SEQN. code: analytic_mort <- nhanes_mortality_link(analytic)  # Key variables added: #   ELIGSTAT     1=eligible, 2=under 18, 3=insufficient data for linkage #   MORTSTAT     0=assumed alive 31-Dec-2019, 1=assumed deceased #   UCOD_LEADING Underlying cause of death (11-category ICD-10 recode) #   PERMTH_EXM   Months from examination date to death or Dec 31 2019 #   PERMTH_INT   Same, from interview date  table(analytic_mort$MORTSTAT, useNA = "always") surv_data <- nhanes_survival_prep(   analytic_mort,   origin     = "exam",   time_unit  = "years",   weight_var = "WTMEC2YR" )  # Follow-up by cycle — note shrinking maximum as cycles approach 2019 nhanes_followup_summary(surv_data) nhanes_ucod_labels()   # see available cause-of-death codes  surv_cvd <- nhanes_survival_prep(   analytic_mort,   origin     = "exam",   time_unit  = "years",   cause      = "001",   # Diseases of heart   weight_var = "WTMEC2YR" )  table(event = surv_cvd$event, cvd_death = surv_cvd$event_cause)

Weight adjustment pooled cycles already handled inside nhanes_survival_prep() weight_var provided. nest = TRUE correct specification NHANES — PSU labels may repeat across strata. Fit Cox model -cause mortality adjusting age, sex, HDL, prior MI, cholesterol-lowering medication: Interpreting output: TC_sd: hazard ratio per one-SD higher total cholesterol, adjusted covariates. direction often reverses adjusting HDL statin use — important confounding structure lipid epidemiology. HDL_sd: higher HDL typically protective (HR < 1). RIAGENDR: coded 1 = male, 2 = female; HR compares females males. MI_history: coded 1 = prior MI, 0 = none; HR estimates excess mortality risk history heart attack. Confounding indication: participants prescribed statin typically higher pre-treatment cholesterol greater cardiovascular risk, statin users sicker average measured TC suggests. Exposure mismeasurement: statins lower TC approximately 30–40 mg/dL, measured TC treated individuals systematically underestimates underlying lipid burden. Including chol_med covariate adjusts group difference recover pre-treatment value. Common analytic responses include restricting analysis untreated participants, imputing pre-treatment TC adding back estimated treatment effect, stratifying medication status reporting separate associations.
code: # Scale continuous predictors to per-SD units for interpretable hazard ratios surv_data$TC_sd  <- scale(surv_data$TC_mgdl)[,  1] surv_data$HDL_sd <- scale(surv_data$HDL_mgdl)[, 1]  design <- svydesign(   id      = ~SDMVPSU,   strata  = ~SDMVSTRA,   weights = ~survey_weight,   nest    = TRUE,   data    = surv_data ) fit <- svycoxph(   Surv(time, event) ~ TC_sd + HDL_sd + RIDAGEYR + RIAGENDR +                       MI_history + chol_med,   design = design )  summary(fit) round(exp(cbind(HR = coef(fit), confint(fit))), 3)

text: nhanesR provides structured workflow downloading, caching, harmonizing, analyzing data National Health Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), including linkage NCHS Public-Use Linked Mortality Files (LMF). package handles main friction points working NHANES: File names change across cycles (e.g. total cholesterol: LAB13 -> L13_B -> L13_C -> TCHOL_D onward). Variable names change across cycles (e.g. HDL: LBDHDL -> LBXHDD -> LBDHDD). SI-unit duplicates appear file alongside conventional-unit columns. Mortality linkage requires fixed-width file parsing SEQN joining across cycles. Lab measurements restricted age: total cholesterol measured participants aged 6 older; fasting analytes (triglycerides, glucose, insulin) require age 12 older. Combined roughly 10-15% enrolled participants complete household interview never attend Mobile Examination Center (MEC), approximately 35-40% participants DEMO file lab measurements. expected design, data loss. LMF restricts mortality follow-participants aged 18 older time survey (ELIGSTAT = 1); nhanes_survival_prep() removes ineligible participants automatically.

title: Survey-Weighted Survival Analysis: Fusing svycoxph and rms
text: NHANES complex probability sample US civilian non-institutionalized population. Valid inference NHANES survival data requires three things standard Cox model implementations provide jointly: Survey-weighted partial likelihood — accounts unequal selection probabilities, stratification, clustering within primary sampling units (PSUs). Ignoring produces standard errors small confidence intervals narrow. Flexible nonlinear covariate effects — biomarkers total cholesterol, GGT, albumin U-shaped threshold relationships mortality. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) capture shapes without requiring priori categorization. rich output environment — rms/Hmisc ecosystem provides nonlinearity tests (anova.rms()), effect displays (Predict(), plot.Predict()), survival curve plots (survplot()) go far beyond base survival offers. survey package provides svycoxph() (1); rms package provides cph() (2) (3). Neither alone provides three. goal vignette describe implement fusion approach combines survey-correct inference svycoxph() output machinery rms ecosystem.

code: library(nhanesR) library(rms) library(survey) library(survival) library(flextable)  dat <- readRDS("~/Documents/R.code/nhanesR/analytic_survival.rds")  # Analysis population: non-statin users, adults >= 20, landmark > 2yr, # complete GGT / albumin / TC / BMI / PIR dat2 <- subset(dat,   ELIGSTAT == 1 & !is.na(time) & time > 2 & statin == FALSE &   !is.na(GGT) & !is.na(LBXSAL) & !is.na(TC) &   !is.na(BMI) & !is.na(INDFMPIR) & RIDAGEYR >= 20 ) # N = 34,456  events = 3,975 # NHANES design: create on the FULL dataset, then subset the design object. # Creating the design on the already-subsetted data can leave some strata with # a single PSU, causing svycoxph() to fail at variance estimation. full_design <- svydesign(   ids     = ~SDMVPSU,   strata  = ~SDMVSTRA,   weights = ~WTMEC2YR,   nest    = TRUE,   data    = dat ) sub_design <- subset(full_design,   ELIGSTAT == 1 & !is.na(time) & time > 2 & statin == FALSE &   !is.na(GGT) & !is.na(LBXSAL) & !is.na(TC) &   !is.na(BMI) & !is.na(INDFMPIR) & RIDAGEYR >= 20 )  # NOTE: this chunk uses raw WTMEC2YR directly for illustration. # For pooled-cycle workflows built via nhanes_survival_prep(weight_var = ...), # use the already-adjusted survey_weight column from that output instead of # applying additional manual cycle scaling. # Shared formula: RCS(4 knots) on GGT and albumin; linear adjusters f <- Surv(time, event) ~ rcs(GGT, 4) + rcs(LBXSAL, 4) +        RIDAGEYR + RIAGENDR + RIDRETH1 + log(BMI)  # cph() fit — x=TRUE, y=TRUE, surv=TRUE needed for Predict() and survplot() # Inference from this fit is NOT survey-correct; used only for $Design structure dd <- datadist(dat2) options(datadist = "dd") fit_cph <- cph(f, data = dat2, x = TRUE, y = TRUE, surv = TRUE)  # svycoxph() fit — survey-correct coefficients and sandwich vcov fit_svy <- svycoxph(f, design = sub_design) names(fit_cph) names(fit_svy)

title: Comparing Survival Frameworks: Cox, Piecewise Exponential, and mgcv-Poisson
text: simulation generates Weibull-proportional-hazards data method Bender, Augustin & Blettner (2005): draw U∼Unif(0,1)U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1) invert cumulative hazard H(t∣x)=(t/scale)shapeexp⁡(x⊤β)H(t \mid x) = (t/\text{scale})^{\text{shape}} \exp(x^\top\beta) get T=scale⋅(−log⁡(U)⋅exp⁡(−x⊤β))1/shape T = \text{scale} \cdot \bigl(-\log(U) \cdot \exp(-x^\top\beta)\bigr)^{1/\text{shape}} Confirmed validation run (true βx1=0.5\beta_{x1} = 0.5, βx2=−0.7\beta_{x2} = -0.7): Cox gives (0.498,−0.673)(0.498, -0.673), PEM K=29K = 29 intervals gives (0.498,−0.673)(0.498, -0.673) — matching Cox three decimals, profile-likelihood equivalence predicts — mgcv-Poisson (REML-selected effective df ≈5\approx 5 smooth baseline hazard) gives (0.490,−0.663)(0.490, -0.663), close identical, consistent targeting penalized rather exactly-profiled baseline hazard.
code: set.seed(20260809)  n <- 3000 x1 <- rnorm(n) x2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)  beta_true  <- c(x1 = 0.5, x2 = -0.7) shape_true <- 1.6 scale_true <- 8  lp      <- beta_true["x1"] * x1 + beta_true["x2"] * x2 u       <- runif(n) t_event <- scale_true * (-log(u) * exp(-lp))^(1 / shape_true) t_cens  <- runif(n, 0, 15)  dat <- data.frame(   time   = pmin(t_event, t_cens),   status = as.integer(t_event <= t_cens),   x1     = x1,   x2     = x2 )  mean(dat$status)  # observed event rate #> [1] 0.4563333 library(survival)  fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x1 + x2, data = dat) summary(fit_cox) #> Call: #> coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ x1 + x2, data = dat) #>  #>   n= 3000, number of events= 1369  #>  #>        coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)     #> x1  0.49767   1.64489  0.02893  17.20   <2e-16 *** #> x2 -0.67270   0.51033  0.05552 -12.12   <2e-16 *** #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 #>  #>    exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95 #> x1    1.6449     0.6079    1.5542     1.741 #> x2    0.5103     1.9595    0.4577     0.569 #>  #> Concordance= 0.656  (se = 0.008 ) #> Likelihood ratio test= 421.6  on 2 df,   p=<2e-16 #> Wald test            = 410.9  on 2 df,   p=<2e-16 #> Score (logrank) test = 414.9  on 2 df,   p=<2e-16 # Person-interval expansion at a moderately fine grid cutpoints <- seq(0.5, 15, by = 0.5)  long <- survSplit(   Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = dat,   cut     = cutpoints,   start   = "tstart",   end     = "tstop",   event   = "event_split",   episode = "interval" ) long$exposure <- long$tstop - long$tstart  fit_pem <- glm(   event_split ~ factor(interval) + x1 + x2,   family = poisson(),   offset = log(exposure),   data   = long )  # Compare only the x1/x2 coefficients to the Cox fit — factor(interval) # terms are the nuisance step-function baseline hazard coef(fit_pem)[c("x1", "x2")] #>         x1         x2  #>  0.4981177 -0.6731074 coef(fit_cox) #>         x1         x2  #>  0.4976738 -0.6726999 library(mgcv) #> Loading required package: nlme #> This is mgcv 1.9-4. For overview type '?mgcv'.  long$tmid <- (long$tstart + long$tstop) / 2  fit_gam <- gam(   event_split ~ s(tmid, bs = "ps", k = 15) + x1 + x2,   family = poisson(),   offset = log(exposure),   data   = long,   method = "REML" )  coef(fit_gam)[c("x1", "x2")] #>         x1         x2  #>  0.4899279 -0.6628936 summary(fit_gam)$edf   # effective df spent on the smooth baseline hazard #> [1] 5.130868

code: widths <- c(4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25)  convergence <- do.call(rbind, lapply(widths, function(w) {   cuts <- seq(w, 15, by = w)   ll <- survSplit(     Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = dat,     cut = cuts, start = "tstart", end = "tstop",     event = "event_split", episode = "interval"   )   ll$exposure <- ll$tstop - ll$tstart   f <- glm(event_split ~ factor(interval) + x1 + x2,            family = poisson(), offset = log(exposure), data = ll)   b <- coef(f)[c("x1", "x2")]   data.frame(     interval_width = w,     n_intervals     = length(cuts),     x1_pem = b["x1"], x2_pem = b["x2"],     x1_abs_diff = abs(b["x1"] - coef(fit_cox)["x1"]),     x2_abs_diff = abs(b["x2"] - coef(fit_cox)["x2"])   ) }))  convergence #>     interval_width n_intervals    x1_pem     x2_pem  x1_abs_diff  x2_abs_diff #> x1            4.00           3 0.4830214 -0.6477601 0.0146523832 2.493977e-02 #> x11           2.00           7 0.4943078 -0.6676225 0.0033660496 5.077378e-03 #> x12           1.00          15 0.4972539 -0.6714390 0.0004199296 1.260873e-03 #> x13           0.50          30 0.4981177 -0.6731074 0.0004438508 4.075456e-04 #> x14           0.25          60 0.4982605 -0.6727977 0.0005866592 9.786285e-05

what: Baseline cumulative hazard: three estimates, one true curve
title: Comparing Survival Frameworks: Cox, Piecewise Exponential, and mgcv-Poisson
text: Confirmed: plot renders without error, three estimated curves track true dashed curve closely, PEM curve visibly “steppy” chosen interval width mgcv curve smooth construction. Cox (Breslow) PEM curves nearly coincide, consistent profile-likelihood equivalence .
code: # True cumulative hazard from the simulation, at x = 0 H0_true <- function(t) (t / scale_true)^shape_true  # Cox: Breslow cumulative hazard (centered = FALSE -> at x = 0) bh_cox <- basehaz(fit_cox, centered = FALSE)  # PEM: step-function cumulative hazard from the fitted interval intercepts. # factor(interval) uses treatment contrasts, so level 1's absolute # log-hazard is the intercept itself, and every other level's absolute # log-hazard is intercept + its dummy coefficient. cf         <- coef(fit_pem) fac_names  <- grep("^factor\\(interval\\)", names(cf), value = TRUE) alpha_hat  <- c(cf["(Intercept)"], cf["(Intercept)"] + cf[fac_names]) lambda_pem <- exp(as.numeric(alpha_hat)) widths_pem <- diff(c(0, cutpoints)) H0_pem     <- cumsum(lambda_pem * widths_pem)  # mgcv: integrate the fitted smooth hazard on a fine grid (x = 0). # Setting exposure = 1 in newdata zeros the offset (log(1) = 0), so the # "response"-scale prediction is the hazard rate itself, not a count. tgrid   <- seq(0.01, 15, length.out = 500) nd      <- data.frame(tmid = tgrid, x1 = 0, x2 = 0, exposure = 1) haz_gam <- predict(fit_gam, newdata = nd, type = "response") H0_gam  <- cumsum(haz_gam) * diff(tgrid)[1]  plot(bh_cox$time, bh_cox$hazard, type = "s", col = "black", lwd = 2,      xlab = "Time", ylab = "Cumulative baseline hazard",      main = "Three estimates of the baseline cumulative hazard") lines(cutpoints, H0_pem, type = "s", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2) lines(tgrid, H0_gam, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2) curve(H0_true, add = TRUE, col = "grey40", lty = 2, lwd = 2) legend("topleft",        c("Cox (Breslow)", "PEM (step function)", "mgcv-Poisson (smooth)", "True"),        col = c("black", "steelblue", "firebrick", "grey40"),        lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2), lwd = 2)

code: # Regime (a): weight is a function only of a covariate already in the # fitted model. w_modeled <- exp(1.0 * dat$x1)  # Regime (b): weight is a function of the realized outcome itself -- # genuinely informative, and not reducible to "a covariate the model # happens to omit." w_outcome <- exp(1.0 * dat$status) # coxph(weights = ) implements Binder's weighted partial-likelihood point # estimate. Its default standard errors are NOT design/sandwich-corrected # for sampling weights -- that correction is what survey::svycoxph() adds # (see vignettes/survey-weighted-survival.Rmd). This demo is about the # point estimate only. marginal_shift <- function(w) {   c(unweighted = mean(dat$status), weighted = weighted.mean(dat$status, w)) } beta_shift <- function(w) {   fit_w <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x1 + x2, data = dat, weights = w)   rbind(unweighted = coef(fit_cox), weighted = coef(fit_w)) }  marginal_shift(w_modeled)   # regime (a): marginal event rate #> unweighted   weighted  #>  0.4563333  0.5798914 beta_shift(w_modeled)       # regime (a): conditional beta #>                   x1         x2 #> unweighted 0.4976738 -0.6726999 #> weighted   0.5567886 -0.7382848  marginal_shift(w_outcome)   # regime (b): marginal event rate #> unweighted   weighted  #>  0.4563333  0.6952728 beta_shift(w_outcome)       # regime (b): conditional beta #>                   x1         x2 #> unweighted 0.4976738 -0.6726999 #> weighted   0.3799150 -0.5318273 one_rep <- function(n) {   x1_r <- rnorm(n); x2_r <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)   lp_r <- beta_true["x1"] * x1_r + beta_true["x2"] * x2_r   uu   <- runif(n)   te   <- scale_true * (-log(uu) * exp(-lp_r))^(1 / shape_true)   tc   <- runif(n, 0, 15)   d    <- data.frame(time = pmin(te, tc), status = as.integer(te <= tc), x1 = x1_r, x2 = x2_r)    f0 <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x1 + x2, data = d)   fa <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x1 + x2, data = d, weights = exp(1.0 * d$x1))   fb <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x1 + x2, data = d, weights = exp(1.0 * d$status))   c(unw_x1 = unname(coef(f0)["x1"]), a_x1 = unname(coef(fa)["x1"]), b_x1 = unname(coef(fb)["x1"])) }  set.seed(20260809) robustness <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(3000, 24000), function(n) {   r  <- t(replicate(30, one_rep(n)))   m  <- colMeans(r)   se <- apply(r, 2, sd) / sqrt(30)   data.frame(     n = n,     bias_a_modeled_covariate = m["a_x1"] - m["unw_x1"], se_a = se["a_x1"],     bias_b_outcome_dependent = m["b_x1"] - m["unw_x1"], se_b = se["b_x1"]   ) }))  robustness #>           n bias_a_modeled_covariate        se_a bias_b_outcome_dependent #> a_x1   3000             -0.002236370 0.012898458               -0.1155326 #> a_x11 24000             -0.001743511 0.004022859               -0.1160873 #>              se_b #> a_x1  0.005504908 #> a_x11 0.001527180

title: Comparing Survival Frameworks: Cox, Piecewise Exponential, and mgcv-Poisson
text: Two separate equivalences established , compose. First, PEM/mgcv-Poisson converges Cox time partition becomes fine, profiling interval-specific baseline-hazard parameter Poisson likelihood reproduces Cox risk-set ratio exactly (β\beta-free constant). Second, profiling argument holds term--term every contribution carries survey weight, weighted PEM/mgcv-Poisson converges Binder’s (1992) weighted Cox identical limit. practical payoff “Design weights” section : risk-set-sum side Cox/PEM contribution population aggregate weighting corrects — event’s covariate value needs correction — design-based β̂\hat\beta can far robust unweighted fitting design-based μ̂\hat\mu , provided variables driving selection already model — confirmed numerically , merely algebra: modeled-covariate weight left β̂\hat\beta’s asymptotic bias indistinguishable zero across twentyfold increase nn, outcome-dependent weight produced bias stable magnitude shrink. proviso exactly ICC/DEFF screening vignettes/survey-weighted-survival.Rmd checks empirically, document supplies mechanism screening result expected first place. equivalence derived also explains PEM historically attractive “Cox regression using ordinary GLM software” (Whitehead 1980) — efficient partial-likelihood implementations common, fitting Poisson GLM split data practical way get approximately β̂\hat\beta. motivation faded now coxph() fast exact, person-interval data representation introduced turned right substrate different set extensions: baseline hazard parametric penalized function (t,x)(t, x) rather free step function, Poisson-GLM machinery generalizes immediately smooth time-varying effects, random effects, multi-state/competing-risks outcomes via standard GAM mixed-model software — precisely PAMM research program (Bender et al. 2018) , different direction (smooth covariate effects exact Cox likelihood), mgcv::gam(family = cox.ph()). NHANES-style application — smooth biomarker effects, mortality outcome, finite sample sizes unpenalized step-function baseline hazard need many intervals look smooth — mgcv-Poisson / PAMM route offers genuine alternative rms::cph() + restricted cubic splines cases smooth baseline hazard curve (just smooth covariate effects) scientific interest, cost losing exact semiparametric guarantee makes Cox regression attractive first place.

title: Urinary Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio Across NHANES Cycles
text: Urinary albumin--creatinine ratio (UACR) key marker chronic kidney disease (CKD) cardiovascular risk. NHANES measured urinary albumin (URXUMA) across ten continuous cycles (1999–2018), making well suited pooled multi-cycle survival analyses. vignette illustrates two practical challenges arise assembling UACR NHANES: File disambiguation: urinary creatinine (URXUCR) appears multiple laboratory files per cycle. early cycles measured albumin/creatinine file several environmental-exposure files (phthalates, heavy metals). nhanes_variable_map() may find wrong file; show use keep_vars pin correct source. Method comparability: NCHS changed urinary albumin assay analyser platform cycles. pooling, analysts consult NHANES laboratory methods documents cycle apply published bridging equations.

title: Urinary Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio Across NHANES Cycles
text: early-cycle rows point files PHPYPA (1999–2000) SSNO3P_B (2001–2002). source want. solution simpler first appears: nhanes_download_analyte() downloads complete file cycle, just named variable. albumin/creatinine files (LAB16, L16_B, L16_C, ALB_CR_*) contain URXUMA URXUCR together, downloading via URXUMA gives us variables single pass.
code: library(nhanesR)  # Confirm URXUMA is present across all ten cycles nhanes_search_variables("albumin", component = "Laboratory")  # Variable map for urinary albumin: maps cleanly to ALB_CR_* files map_uma <- nhanes_variable_map("URXUMA") map_uma # nhanes_variable_map("URXUCR") resolves to the wrong file in early cycles: # URXUCR appears in phthalates / heavy-metals files (e.g. PHPYPA 1999-2000) # as a dilution-adjustment variable, and the catalog finds those first. nhanes_variable_map("URXUCR")

title: Urinary Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio Across NHANES Cycles
code: # Restrict to cycles with public-use mortality linkage (1999-2018) cycles <- nhanes_cycles()[nhanes_cycles()$has_lmf_public, "cycle"]  # nhanes_download_analyte resolves the changing file name automatically. # Each returned data frame contains the full ALB_CR file — including # URXUMA (urinary albumin) AND URXUCR (urinary creatinine). alb_cr_list <- nhanes_download_analyte("URXUMA", cycles) alb_cr      <- nhanes_stack(alb_cr_list)

title: Urinary Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio Across NHANES Cycles
text: NHANES reports: conversion mg/g : UACR (mg/g)=URXUMA (mg/L)URXUCR (mg/dL)×0.01 (g/dL per mg/dL)=100×URXUMAURXUCR\text{UACR (mg/g)} = \frac{\text{URXUMA (mg/L)}}{\text{URXUCR (mg/dL)} \times 0.01 \text{ (g/dL per mg/dL)}} = \frac{100 \times \text{URXUMA}}{\text{URXUCR}}

title: Urinary Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio Across NHANES Cycles

code: library(survival) library(survey)  # Link mortality alb_cr_mort <- nhanes_mortality_link(alb_cr) alb_cr_surv <- nhanes_survival_prep(   alb_cr_mort,   origin     = "exam",   time_unit  = "years",   weight_var = "WTMEC2YR" )  # Survey design options(survey.lonely.psu = "adjust") svy <- svydesign(   ids     = ~SDMVPSU,   strata  = ~SDMVSTRA,   weights = ~survey_weight,   nest    = TRUE,   data    = alb_cr_surv )  # Unadjusted rate by UACR category svyby(~event, ~UACR_cat, svy, svymean, na.rm = TRUE)

text: nhanesR provides structured workflow working NHANES (National Health Nutrition Examination Survey) public-use data NCHS Public-Use Linked Mortality Files (LMF). handles main friction points multi-cycle NHANES analysis: File names change across cycles (e.g. total cholesterol: LAB13 → L13_B → L13_C → TCHOL_D onward) Variable names change across cycles (e.g. HDL: LBDHDL → LBXHDD → LBDHDD) SI-unit duplicate columns appear alongside conventional-unit columns file Mortality linkage requires fixed-width file parsing SEQN joining across cycles

title: Download, Parse, and Analyze NHANES Data with Mortality Linkage
code: library(nhanesR)  # 1. Find available cycles cycles <- nhanes_cycles()[["cycle"]]   # character vector of all cycle labels  # 2. Browse files available in a cycle nhanes_manifest("2015-2016", "Laboratory")  # 3. Search the variable catalog by keyword nhanes_search_variables("total cholesterol", component = "Laboratory") nhanes_variable_map("total cholesterol")   # per-cycle file/variable lookup  # 4. Download — use nhanes_download_analyte() when file names changed across cycles demo_list  <- nhanes_download("DEMO", cycles[1:10])          # stable name tchol_list <- nhanes_download_analyte("total cholesterol",   # resolves renames                                        cycles[1:10])  # 5. Harmonize variable names and stack into one data frame TC <- nhanes_harmonize(tchol_list,                         unit          = "mg/dL",                         name          = "TC_mgdl",                         label_pattern = "total cholesterol")  # 6. Merge components by SEQN demo   <- nhanes_stack(demo_list) analytic <- nhanes_merge(demo, TC, by = c("SEQN", "cycle"))  # 7. Link mortality follow-up (through December 31, 2019) analytic_mort <- nhanes_mortality_link(analytic)  # 8. Prepare survival dataset surv_data <- nhanes_survival_prep(analytic_mort,                                    origin     = "exam",                                    time_unit  = "years",                                    weight_var = "WTMEC2YR")

title: Download and cache NHANES XPT data files — nhanes_download
text: File codes base names CDC assigns data file, without cycle-letter suffix .xpt extension. example, Demographics file always "DEMO", blood pressure examination file "BPX". Use nhanes_manifest() browse files available given cycle component. file_name column manifest shows full CDC name including cycle suffix (e.g. "TCHOL_I"); strip trailing underscore-letter get base code nhanes_download():   Note analyte file names changed across cycles (e.g. total cholesterol: LAB13 -> L13_B -> TCHOL_D onward). cases, use nhanes_download_analyte() instead, looks correct CDC filename cycle automatically via variable catalog.
code: m <- nhanes_manifest("2015-2016", "Laboratory") m[, c("file_name", "description")]  # Base codes ready for nhanes_download(): sub("_[A-Z]$", "", m$file_name)

title: Download and cache NHANES XPT data files — nhanes_download
text: File codes validated download attempt. unknown code supplied, CDC returns HTTP 200 HTML error page rather 404. nhanesR detects via Content-Type header aborts message directing nhanes_manifest() confirm correct name.

title: Download and cache NHANES XPT data files — nhanes_download
text: NHANES XPT files produced SAS, writes variable labels system locale generating server — typically Latin-1 (ISO 8859-1). biochemistry files (notably BIOPRO predecessors L40_C onward) use Latin-1 byte 0xB5 micro prefix SI unit strings umol/L. byte valid UTF-8, downstream code runs regular expressions label attributes receive "unable translate ... wide string" warning label skipped. nhanesR guards internally passing labels iconv(..., = "UTF-8", sub = "") pattern matching nhanes_harmonize(). read label attributes directly code, apply conversion:
code: labels <- iconv(   vapply(df, function(col) attr(col, "label") %||% "", character(1L)),   to = "UTF-8", sub = "" )

title: Download NHANES files for an analyte using the CDC variable catalog — nhanes_download_analyte
text: smarter alternative nhanes_download() analytes whose file name changed across cycles (e.g. total cholesterol: LAB13 -> L13_B -> L13_C -> TCHOL_D onward). Uses nhanes_variable_map() look correct CDC file name cycle, downloads using exact catalog name.

Default "Laboratory". keep_vars Character vector NULL. Passed nhanes_variable_map() disambiguate serum urine forms analyte. refresh Logical. Re-download even cached? Default FALSE. add_cycle_col Logical. Add cycle column data frame? Default TRUE.

what: Harmonize variable names across NHANES cycles and stack into one data frame — nhanes_harmonize
title: Harmonize variable names across NHANES cycles and stack into one data frame — nhanes_harmonize
text: NHANES analytes sometimes stored different variable names different cycles (e.g. HDL cholesterol: LBDHDL 1999-2002, LBXHDD 2003-2004, LBDHDD 2005 onward). nhanes_harmonize() offers two ways resolve :

title: Harmonize variable names across NHANES cycles and stack into one data frame — nhanes_harmonize
code: nhanes_harmonize(   data_list,   mapping = NULL,   unit = NULL,   name = NULL,   label_pattern = NULL,   units = c("conventional", "SI", "both"),   trim = TRUE,   stack = TRUE )

title: Harmonize variable names across NHANES cycles and stack into one data frame — nhanes_harmonize
text: data_list named list per-cycle data frames, returned nhanes_download() nhanes_download_analyte(). mapping named character vector names old (per-cycle) variable names values single common name use across cycles. Multiple old names may map new name. Example: c(LBDHDL = "HDL_mgdl", LBXHDD = "HDL_mgdl", LBDHDD = "HDL_mgdl"). Ignored unit provided. unit Character NULL. unit string match column label attributes (case-insensitive). Common values: "mg/dL", "g/dL", "U/L", "umol/L". supplied, name must also provided. name Character NULL. output column name use unit supplied (e.g. "HDL_mgdl"). label_pattern Character NULL. additional regex matched column labels unit used. Use disambiguate file contains multiple columns unit (e.g. "HDL" select HDL column file also contains total cholesterol mg/dL). units Character. Controls unit system retain conventional SI versions measurement exist data frame (e.g. LBXTC mg/dL LBDTCSI mmol/L). One : "conventional" (default) Keep mg/dL, g/dL, U/L, etc.; drop SI duplicates. Appropriate US-centric analyses. "SI" Keep mmol/L, g/L, umol/L, etc.; drop conventional duplicates. Appropriate international use journals require SI units. "" Retain columns; duplicates removed. Detection uses label attributes rather variable names CDC naming inconsistent (e.g. LBXTC/LBDTCSI). Applied renaming step. trim Logical. TRUE (default), returned data frame contains SEQN, cycle, harmonized column(s). Set FALSE retain columns (useful source file contains variables want keep). stack Logical. TRUE (default), row-bind renamed data frames single data frame using nhanes_stack(). Set FALSE return renamed list without stacking.

title: Harmonize variable names across NHANES cycles and stack into one data frame — nhanes_harmonize
text: stack = TRUE (default), single stacked data frame. unit used trim = TRUE (default), SEQN, cycle, harmonized column returned – ready merging. stack = FALSE, named list data frames.

title: Harmonize variable names across NHANES cycles and stack into one data frame — nhanes_harmonize
text: Unit-based (unit + name): scans column label attributes specified unit string (e.g. "mg/dL") renames matching column. need know CDC variable codes advance. Use label_pattern disambiguate file contains multiple columns unit (e.g. early cycles bundled total cholesterol HDL together). Explicit mapping (mapping): named character vector old -> new variable names. verbose unambiguous.

title: Harmonize variable names across NHANES cycles and stack into one data frame — nhanes_harmonize
code: # \donttest{ cycles <- nhanes_cycles()[1:10, "cycle"]  # Conventional units (default): returns SEQN + cycle + HDL_mgdl hdl_list <- nhanes_download_analyte("HDL", cycles) #> Found 11 unique variables matching "HDL". #> Warning: Both "2017-2018" and "2017-2020" are present. The 2017-2018 participants are #> included in the 2017-2020 pandemic-adjusted file -- use one or the other in #> pooled analyses to avoid double-counting. hdl <- nhanes_harmonize(hdl_list, unit = "mg/dL", name = "HDL_mgdl",                          label_pattern = "HDL")  # SI units: retain mmol/L columns, drop conventional duplicates hdl_si <- nhanes_harmonize(hdl_list, unit = "mmol/L", name = "HDL_mmol",                             label_pattern = "HDL", units = "SI")  # Merge two analytes cleanly tchol_list <- nhanes_download_analyte("total cholesterol", cycles) #> Found 6 unique variables matching "total cholesterol". #> Warning: Both "2017-2018" and "2017-2020" are present. The 2017-2018 participants are #> included in the 2017-2020 pandemic-adjusted file -- use one or the other in #> pooled analyses to avoid double-counting. TC  <- nhanes_harmonize(tchol_list, unit = "mg/dL", name = "TC_mgdl",                          label_pattern = "total cholesterol") lipids <- merge(hdl, TC, by = c("SEQN", "cycle"))  # Explicit mapping hdl <- nhanes_harmonize(   hdl_list,   mapping = c(LBDHDL = "HDL_mgdl", LBXHDD = "HDL_mgdl",               LBDHDD = "HDL_mgdl") ) # }

what: Merge NHANES component data frames by SEQN — nhanes_merge
title: Merge NHANES component data frames by SEQN — nhanes_merge
text: Joins two NHANES data frames SEQN respondent sequence number. Validates survey design variables (PSU, strata, weights) present warns merging across components use different weight variables.

title: Merge NHANES component data frames by SEQN — nhanes_merge
code: nhanes_merge(..., by = "SEQN", type = c("inner", "left"), weight_var = NULL)

title: Merge NHANES component data frames by SEQN — nhanes_merge
text: ... Two data frames nhanes_download(), containing SEQN column. multi-cycle datasets, also cycle column. Character vector join key(s). Default "SEQN". multi-cycle data, use c("SEQN", "cycle"). type Character. Join type: "inner" retains participants present files; "left" retains participants first file. Default "inner" (standard NHANES analytic approach). weight_var Character NULL. supplied, validates weight column exists merged result.

title: Merge NHANES component data frames by SEQN — nhanes_merge
text: merged data frame. Duplicate columns (present one input) deduplicated, keeping version first data frame column appears, warning.

title: Merge NHANES component data frames by SEQN — nhanes_merge
text: appropriate weight depends components merged: Demographics -> WTINT2YR (interview weight) exam/lab component -> WTMEC2YR (MEC exam weight) Dietary 24-hr recall -> WTDRD1 WTDR2D Multi-cycle pooled -> divide 2-year weight number cycles, use 4-year combined weight available function warns enforce weight selection. Use nhanes_cycles() look available weight variable names per cycle.

title: Merge NHANES component data frames by SEQN — nhanes_merge
code: # \donttest{ demo  <- nhanes_download("DEMO",  "2015-2016") bpx   <- nhanes_download("BPX",   "2015-2016") trigly <- nhanes_download("TRIGLY","2015-2016")  analytic <- nhanes_merge(demo, bpx, trigly) #> Warning: ! Some inputs have a "cycle" column but `by` does not include "'cycle'". #> ℹ For multi-cycle data, use `by = c('SEQN', 'cycle')` to avoid cross-cycle #>   contamination. #> Warning: ! Duplicate column in merge step 2: "cycle". #> ℹ Keeping the version from the first data frame. Rename columns before merging #>   if both are needed. #> Warning: ! Duplicate column in merge step 3: "cycle". #> ℹ Keeping the version from the first data frame. Rename columns before merging #>   if both are needed.  # Multi-cycle: use nhanes_stack() before merging demo_list <- nhanes_download("DEMO", c("2013-2014", "2015-2016")) bpx_list  <- nhanes_download("BPX",  c("2013-2014", "2015-2016")) demo_pool <- nhanes_stack(demo_list) bpx_pool  <- nhanes_stack(bpx_list) analytic  <- nhanes_merge(demo_pool, bpx_pool, by = c("SEQN", "cycle")) # }

what: Download NHANES Public-Use Linked Mortality Files — nhanes_mortality_download
title: Download NHANES Public-Use Linked Mortality Files — nhanes_mortality_download
text: Downloads fixed-width .dat mortality files CDC FTP server one NHANES cycles. Files cached locally; re-downloading skipped unless refresh = TRUE.

title: Download NHANES Public-Use Linked Mortality Files — nhanes_mortality_download
code: nhanes_mortality_download(   cycles = NULL,   refresh = FALSE,   quiet = !getOption("nhanesR.verbose", TRUE) )

title: Download NHANES Public-Use Linked Mortality Files — nhanes_mortality_download
text: cycles Character vector cycle labels. Defaults cycles public-use LMF. See nhanes_cycles() nhanes_lmf_cycles(). refresh Logical. Re-download even cached file exists? Default FALSE. quiet Logical. Suppress download messages? Default uses nhanesR.verbose option.

title: Download NHANES Public-Use Linked Mortality Files — nhanes_mortality_download
text: Invisibly, named character vector local file paths (one per cycle). primary side-effect writing files cache directory mortality/dat/.

title: Download NHANES Public-Use Linked Mortality Files — nhanes_mortality_download
text: public-use LMF provides mortality follow-December 31, 2019 NHANES 1999-2018 NHANES III. Files released April 2022 updated (2022-linked restricted-use files require RDC access).

title: Download NHANES Public-Use Linked Mortality Files — nhanes_mortality_download
code: # \donttest{ # Download all available cycles nhanes_mortality_download()  # Download specific cycles nhanes_mortality_download(c("2013-2014", "2015-2016", "2017-2018")) # }

what: Link mortality data onto an NHANES analytic dataset — nhanes_mortality_link
title: Link mortality data onto an NHANES analytic dataset — nhanes_mortality_link
text: Performs left join parsed LMF onto data frame containing NHANES participants, matched participant sequence number. Automatically handles multiple cycles row-binding appropriate LMF files joining.

title: Link mortality data onto an NHANES analytic dataset — nhanes_mortality_link
code: nhanes_mortality_link(   nhanes_data,   cycles = NULL,   keep_vars = NULL,   download = TRUE,   seqn_col = "SEQN",   cycle_col = "cycle" )

title: Link mortality data onto an NHANES analytic dataset — nhanes_mortality_link
text: nhanes_data data frame containing NHANES participants. cycles Character vector "YYYY-YYYY" cycle labels present nhanes_data. Inferred cycle_col omitted. keep_vars Character vector LMF variables retain. Defaults : c("ELIGSTAT", "MORTSTAT", "UCOD_LEADING", "DIABETES", "HYPERTEN", "PERMTH_INT", "PERMTH_EXM"). download Logical. Download missing LMF files automatically? Default TRUE. seqn_col Character. Name participant sequence-number column nhanes_data. Default "SEQN" (nhanesR / CDC standard). Use "seqn" nhanesdata output. cycle_col Character. Name cycle column nhanes_data. Default "cycle" ("YYYY-YYYY" labels). Use "year" nhanesdata output, column contains integer start years (e.g. 1999, 2001).

title: Link mortality data onto an NHANES analytic dataset — nhanes_mortality_link
text: nhanes_data LMF columns appended. Rows mortality record (SEQNs absent LMF) NA LMF columns; occur continuous NHANES 1999-2018.

title: Link mortality data onto an NHANES analytic dataset — nhanes_mortality_link
text: Data source – nhanes_download(), nhanesA, nhanesdata – can linked supplying appropriate column name arguments. example, nhanesdata stores sequence number seqn (integer) cycle year (integer start year, e.g. 1999); pass seqn_col = "seqn", cycle_col = "year" handled automatically.

title: Link mortality data onto an NHANES analytic dataset — nhanes_mortality_link
code: # \donttest{ demo <- nhanes_download("DEMO", "2015-2016") demo_mort <- nhanes_mortality_link(demo) # }

what: Parse NHANES Linked Mortality Files into data frames — nhanes_mortality_parse
title: Parse NHANES Linked Mortality Files into data frames — nhanes_mortality_parse
text: Reads fixed-width .dat files (downloading first needed) returns named list data frames, one per cycle.

title: Parse NHANES Linked Mortality Files into data frames — nhanes_mortality_parse
code: nhanes_mortality_parse(cycles = NULL, refresh = FALSE, download = TRUE)

title: Parse NHANES Linked Mortality Files into data frames — nhanes_mortality_parse
text: cycles Character vector cycle labels. Defaults available. refresh Logical. Re-parse even cached RDS exists? Default FALSE. download Logical. Auto-download missing .dat files? Default TRUE.

title: Parse NHANES Linked Mortality Files into data frames — nhanes_mortality_parse
text: named list data frames. data frame contains: SEQN Respondent sequence number (join key NHANES data). ELIGSTAT Eligibility: 1=eligible; 2=18; 3=insufficient data. MORTSTAT Vital status: 0=assumed alive; 1=assumed deceased. UCOD_LEADING Underlying cause death (11-category ICD-10 recode). DIABETES Diabetes mentioned death certificate (1=yes). title: Prepare an NHANES-LMF dataset for survival analysis — nhanes_survival_prep
text: NHANES provides three families survey weight, correcting different sampling stage. Choosing wrong weight produces biased point estimates incorrect standard errors. fasting subsample weight (WTSAF2YR) statistical probability weight – body-weight measurement – accounts additional random subsampling participants asked fast blood draw. Fasting participants minority MEC attendees; using WTMEC2YR fasting analytes ignores extra subsampling step give incorrect population estimates. pooled multi-cycle analyses, CDC guidance scales weights number pooled cycles (n). function applies automatically 2-year weight supplied: 1999-2000 2001-2002 present corresponding 4-year weight column exists (e.g., WTMEC4YR WTMEC2YR), two early cycles scaled 4-year weight * (2/n). later cycles scaled 2-year weight * (1/n). early-pair 4-year weight column unavailable, cycles fall back 2-year weight * (1/n). original unscaled 2-year weight preserved survey_weight_2yr_raw.

title: Compute survey-weighted cumulative baseline hazard with variance — weighted_basehaz
text: Implements weighted Breslow estimator linearization-based variance following Lin (2000). point estimate weights event's contribution survey weight; variance uses influence function weighted estimator combined survey design's stratified cluster structure.

title: Compute survey-weighted cumulative baseline hazard with variance — weighted_basehaz
text: fit_svy fitted svycoxph object. design svydesign object used fit fit_svy. centered Logical. TRUE (default), baseline hazard corresponds person weighted mean covariate, matching centered=TRUE default survival::basehaz(). se_type Character. variance estimator use std.err: "lin" (default) Lin (2000) design-based linearization variance. Measures sensitivity PSU selection; appropriate population-level design inference. Produces small SEs large-population surveys like NHANES. "greenwood" Survey-weighted Greenwood formula: \(\sum_{t_k \leq t} n^w(t_k) / [Y^w(t_k)]^2\). Measures statistical precision weighted event count; gives confidence bands interpretable width survplot().

title: Compute survey-weighted cumulative baseline hazard with variance — weighted_basehaz
text: data frame columns: time Event times. hazard Weighted cumulative baseline hazard H_0(t). surv Baseline survival exp(-H_0(t)). se_H0 Standard error H_0(t) hazard scale. std.err Standard error log(H_0(t)), direct substitution $std.err slot fused cph object. Computed se_H0 via delta method: SE(log H) = SE(H)/H.

title: Compute survey-weighted cumulative baseline hazard with variance — weighted_basehaz
text: weighted Breslow increment event time \(t_k\) : $$d\hat{H}_0^w(t_k) = \frac{\sum_{: t_i = t_k, \delta_i=1} w_i}   {\sum_{j \\mathcal{R}(t_k)} w_j \exp(\mathbf{X}_j^\top \hat{\beta})}$$ influence function \(d\hat{H}_0^w(t_k)\) observation \(\) (Lin 2000, eq. 2.3): $$\phi_i(t_k) = \frac{(t_i = t_k,\, \delta_i = 1)}{Y^w(t_k)} -   \frac{n^w(t_k)}{[Y^w(t_k)]^2}\, (t_i \geq t_k)\, \exp(\mathbf{X}_i^\top\hat{\beta})$$ \(Y^w(t_k) = \sum_{j \\mathcal{R}(t_k)} w_j \exp(\mathbf{X}_j^\top\hat{\beta})\) \(n^w(t_k) = \sum_{: t_i=t_k, \delta_i=1} w_i\). cumulative influence \(\Phi_i(t) = \sum_{t_k \leq t} \phi_i(t_k)\) used construct linearization variance estimate (Lin 2000, eq. 2.4): $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{H}_0^w(t)) =   \sum_h \frac{n_h}{n_h - 1}   \sum_{\alpha \h} \left(e_{h\alpha}(t) - \bar{e}_h(t)\right)^2$$ \(e_{h\alpha}(t) = \sum_{\\text{PSU}\,\alpha} \Phi_i(t)\) PSU-level total influence functions within stratum \(h\). Note: variance conditions \(\hat{\beta}\) propagate uncertainty coefficient estimation. large samples contribution negligible relative design variance.

title: Compute survey-weighted cumulative baseline hazard with variance — weighted_basehaz
text: NHANES-scale populations Lin design variance orders magnitude smaller Greenwood-weighted variance former captures PSU-selection uncertainty (small rare events), latter captures statistical uncertainty weighted event count. ratio approximately proportional square root mean survey weight. Use se_type = "greenwood" goal survplot() confidence bands convey statistical reliability; use "lin" goal design-consistent variance formal population inference.

Unlike NHANES’s SEQN, NHIS’s PUBLICID confirmed unique across survey years, nhis_mortality_link() matches (PUBLICID, year) rather ID alone. nhis_survival_prep(): NHIS LMF PERMTH_INT/PERMTH_EXM-equivalent person-months variable, DODQTR/DODYEAR, follow-time construction requires NHIS interview date survey data .

title: nhanesR 0.1.0
text: nhanes_cycles() — list continuous NHANES cycles (1999–present) optionally NHANES III (1988–1994), cycle labels, begin/end years, file-name suffixes. nhanes_manifest() — query CDC data catalog available files within given cycle component. nhanes_download() — download one NHANES XPT files CDC, parse R data frames, cache locally. Falls back foreign::read.xport() haven::read_xpt() parse older files. nhanes_stack() — row-bind per-cycle data frames single data frame, filling columns absent cycles NA. nhanes_merge() — join NHANES components SEQN (optionally cycle), survey-design-aware defaults. nhanes_mortality_link() — download NCHS Public-Use Linked Mortality Files (LMF) relevant cycles left-join onto analytic dataset SEQN. Mortality follow-runs December 31, 2019. nhanes_survival_prep() — prepare survival analysis dataset mortality-linked data frame: removes ineligible participants (ELIGSTAT != 1), creates time event columns, optionally creates event_cause cause-specific mortality, warns asymmetric follow-across cycles. nhanes_followup_summary() — summarize follow-time event rates cycle. nhanes_ucod_labels() — return 11-category ICD-10 underlying cause-- death recode used public-use LMF. nhanes_search_variables() — search CDC NHANES variable catalog variables whose name description matches keyword. Results cached locally. summarize argument (default TRUE) collapses one-row-per-cycle output one row per unique variable name, comma-separated file names, cycles, n_cycles count. nhanes_variable_map() — wraps nhanes_search_variables() return single-row-per-cycle lookup table (cycle, variable_name, file_name) given analyte. Automatically drops comment-code variables, prefers non-SI variables exist cycle, accepts keep_vars argument disambiguate serum urine forms analyte (e.g. serum creatinine vs. urinary creatinine). nhanes_cache_dir() — view change local cache directory.
